query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introduction of a controlled, optimized thermal treatment to the high-entropy alloy will reduce post-exposure toughness degradation by stabilizing the grain structure and preventing deleterious phase transformations.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 500-800°C, Duration: 1-10 hours, Loading: minimal or no external stress
generation.mechanism: Stabilization of grain boundaries and prevention of deleterious phase transformations
generation.predicted_outcome: Retained strength-ductility combination and reduced toughness degradation after service-relevant heating
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with identical composition and processing history
generation.boundary: Temperature: 500-800°C, Duration: 1-10 hours, Loading: minimal or no external stress
generation.uncertainty: Optimization of thermal treatment parameters and potential interactions with other microstructural features

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of thermally treated and untreated high-entropy alloys under service-relevant heating conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated alloy exhibits significantly reduced toughness or altered microstructure compared to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys consist of alloying elements with five or more equal molar fractions, each of which has a molar fraction of about 5% to 35%. As a kind of comprehensive material, high entropy alloy has better physical and chemical properties than many common metal compounds []. Therefore, it has attracted wide attention in material science and engineering and is the focus field of scholars at home and abroad [,]. In recent years, many scholars at home and abroad have used high entropy alloys for surface modification, mainly by laser melting, laser deposition, and plasma melting. The lower preparation cost and excellent performance of high entropy alloys not only improve their service life and significantly reduce the failure loss but also reduce their surface repair cost, and high entropy alloys have many advantages that traditional alloys can hardly match []. However, there are difficulties in the synergistic enhancement of strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance of high entropy alloys, and no satisfactory solution has been found so far []. The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). High-entropy alloys (HEAs) constitute one of the most innovative classes of metallic materials, attracting significant attention from both scientific and industrial communities in recent years [,,]. Their uniqueness lies in the design of chemical composition, where several principal elements are present in nearly equimolar proportions, leading to the formation of high-entropy phases with simplified crystalline structures [,]. These materials exhibit exceptional mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties, often surpassing those of traditional engineering alloys [,]. HEAs, particularly the Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi), remain among the most recognized and extensively studied representatives within this group []. Since its discovery, the Cantor alloy has attracted significant scientific attention due to its exceptional mechanical properties, distinguishing it from both conventional and other HEAs [,]. It exhibits a single-phase FCC structure with excellent ductility and resistance to brittle fracture, even under cryogenic conditions [,,]. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. The concept of high entropy alloy (HEA) was proposed and published in 2004 [,,] and the unique properties of these alloys have attracted attention from research groups all over the world. The pioneering studies by Cantor et al. were the first to report that an equiatomic alloy consisting of the five transition metals Cr, Mn, Fe, Co and Ni crystallized as a single solid solution [,] in the as-cast and in the homogenized state. The first HEA generation could contain five or more main elements with the concentration of each element in the range 5–35 at. % []. The alloys presented a high mixing entropy in their liquid state [] and thus could form simple solid solution structures (e.g., FCC, BCC and HCP) in place of intermetallic phases. Some promising technological characteristics of HEAs were high hardness [], good wear resistance [], excellent strength at both high and low temperatures [,,] and generally a good resistance to oxidation and corrosion [].
